description: We are two experienced technologists and makers who are passionate about science and space. We are creative and pragmatic.
summary:
The Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer is a free and open browser game that puts children aged 7–12 in charge of a three-astronaut lunar outpost for a seven-day mission. Players run a realistic mission-control console - managing solar panels, an oxygen electrolyser, CO₂ scrubbing and a radiation shelter - while real NASA space-weather data (from the DONKI API) determines each day's dangers.

The game makes engineering trade-offs tangible: making oxygen consumes  the water supply and drains power; the storm shelter protects the crew but costs energy; running experiments advances the mission but competes with life support. If power, oxygen or crew safety reaches zero, the crew must be rescued — children learn that engineering means balancing competing demands under constraint.


Three graduated missions, plain-language "Learn" cards, and "today → tomorrow" projections make complex systems approachable without oversimplifying; where the game simplifies, it says so honestly. To complete the experience we have provided a live space-weather dashboard and  astronomy picture archive (using NASA APIs), printable achievement certificates and a leader board. Furthermore live data from local sensors adds an extra real-time dimension.

Space STEM content usually entertains without teaching, or teaches without engaging. This project closes that gap turning "space is cool" into "I kept three astronauts alive, and I understand how."
details:
What it does and how it works

Children aged 7–12 command a three-astronaut lunar outpost for a seven-day mission. From a mission-control console they operate real systems — solar panels, an oxygen electrolyser, CO₂ scrubber and radiation shelter — balancing power, oxygen and crew safety gauges. Crucially, each day's dangers come from real NASA space-weather data (the DONKI API): actual solar flares and magnetic storms from historical event weeks drive the game's storms. Players see "today → tomorrow" projections before committing to decisions, face equipment faults and debris drills, and earn a printable achievement certificate. If any gauge hits zero, the crew must be rescued.

Benefits

It makes invisible engineering trade-offs felt: making oxygen consumes the water supply; the shelter saves lives but drains power; science competes with survival. Plain-language "Learn" cards explain every machine, and the game honestly labels where it simplifies. It is free, runs in any browser, and needs no installation.

Intended impact

To close the gap between space content that entertains without teaching and content that teaches without engaging — turning "space is cool" into "I kept three astronauts alive, and I understand how." A live sensor page (temperature, humidity, light, CO₂ fed by a real webhook) extends the habitat into the physical classroom.

Tools and technology

Built with React, TypeScript, TanStack Start and Tailwind CSS on the Lovable platform; Lovable Cloud (Supabase) provides the database, live updates and webhook API; NASA's DONKI and astronomy-picture APIs supply real data; pdf-lib generates certificates. Extensive automated tests keep the game rules reliable.

Creativity

Real NASA data as the game's weather engine, honest labelling of simulated events, a physical-sensor link, and a generative AI-assisted development process (SI) — a creative blend of live science, gameplay and real hardware.

Factors we considered

Age-appropriate language and stakes (rescue, never death); scientific accuracy versus playability; accessibility and zero cost; data honesty; and replayability through rotating historical event weeks.

Most space games invent their dangers. Ours are real,.every storm in the game actually happened, recorded by NASA's own instruments. When a solar storm is a day away and the shelter needs the same power as the oxygen generator, children don't just learn about engineering trade-offs, they have to make one. It is honest about what's real and what's simplified, and can link to real classroom sensors. Any child can play it today and discover for themselves what it takes to keep astronauts alive.
